title: Beacons in the fog
subtitle: DNS rhythm, address ranges, and which way the bytes went
intro: Every ten minutes since 19:40, AUTOMATION-01 has asked the same question of DNS and made the same small connection. That rhythm is a scheduled task talking to whoever owns 203.0.113.44. Network events carry direction: principal is the side that started it, target is the side that answered. Read them that way and the night's traffic tells its own story.
concepts: CIDR notation names a range of addresses
Parentheses decide what OR applies to
sent_bytes is from the principal's point of view
recap: Recognise a fixed interval in a count as a beacon, not a person
Test an IP field against a CIDR range with net.ip_in_range_cidr
Wrap an OR in parentheses so it stays inside the event-type filter
Compare bytes as numbers and read the direction from the principal's side

missions.title: The same question every ten minutes
missions.beat: Count DNS lookups for anything under the lookalike domain, grouped by the machine asking. One number will stand out.
missions.question: Which machine keeps looking up the lookalike domain, and how often?

concept.title: Regular intervals are a signature
concept.text: People browse in bursts. Scheduled code is punctual. Divide a machine's lookup count by the hours it spans: if it comes out to one every ten minutes, you are looking at the PledgeSync task's /mo 10 interval, not a person refreshing a page.

explain.meaning: Anchored to the end, so cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example and the bare domain both match.
How many lookup events each machine produced.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
network.dns.questions.name = /pier9-partners\.example$/
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $lookups = count(metadata.id)
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
network.dns.questions.name = /pier9-partners\.example$/
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $lookups = count(metadata.id)
hints: Run it. Two machines appear; compare their counts.
Change match to principal.hostname, network.dns.questions.name to see which exact name each machine asked for.
AUTOMATION-01 made 62 lookups for cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example. PLEDGE-DESK-02 made one, at 18:52, for the bare domain.

answer.prompt: How many lookups did AUTOMATION-01 make?

call.prompt: Open the AUTOMATION-01 row's lookups: they are spaced ten minutes apart from 19:40 until nearly 06:00. What is the strongest reading?

options.label: A user kept refreshing the sponsor page all night from the playout PC, which has a browser like any other
A DNS misconfiguration on the playout PC is retrying a name it cannot resolve, once per cache expiry
Automated check-ins from the scheduled task: a beacon that outlived every human on shift

call.why: The spacing matches the task's /mo 10 interval exactly, and the lookups continue long after every human went home.

missions.clue: AUTOMATION-01 called home 62 times. PLEDGE-DESK-02 called once, at 18:52, when Hal followed the link. Two different stories from the same domain: one click, then one machine on a leash.
missions.caveat: Beacons in the wild add jitter and rotate names. A clean ten-minute cadence is a teaching case, not a promise.

missions.title: Connections into the attacker's range
missions.beat: The lookalike resolves to 203.0.113.44. Attackers rarely own one address; they rent a block. Search for connections into the whole /24 on the web port.
missions.question: How many connections went to 203.0.113.0/24 on port 443?

concept.title: CIDR names a range
concept.text: 203.0.113.0/24 means 'the first 24 bits are fixed': every address from 203.0.113.0 to 203.0.113.255. net.ip_in_range_cidr tests an IP field against that range, so you catch neighbours of the one address you already know.

explain.meaning: A function used as a condition. First argument is the IP field, second is the range as a quoted string.
Numbers are unquoted. Port 443 is HTTPS, which hides the content but not the destination.

hints: The connections go to the attacker, so the attacker's address is on the target side.

call.prompt: Every connection in your result used port 443. Does HTTPS make them safer?

options.label: No; encryption hides the content from you too, so destination, timing and volume are your evidence
Yes; encrypted traffic cannot carry stolen data out without breaking the TLS session, which the gateway would log
Yes; port 443 is allowed by the firewall, so whatever used it was approved traffic and is out of scope

call.why: Attackers use 443 because it is allowed everywhere and inspected nowhere. The metadata around the connection is what you can still read.

missions.clue: Sixty-five connections into the range: 63 from AUTOMATION-01, two from PLEDGE-DESK-02 at 18:52 and 18:53. The two from Hal's desk are the page load and the form post. Everything after that is the playout PC.
missions.caveat: The range here is from RFC 5737 documentation space and belongs to nobody. Never put a real indicator from work into a public trainer.

missions.title: Either end of the wire
missions.beat: Hal's workstation is 10.9.4.22. Odalys wants everything it talked to and everything that talked to it. Direction matters, so you have to ask about both roles.
missions.question: How many connections involved 10.9.4.22 in either role?

concept.title: Parentheses decide what OR applies to
concept.text: AND binds tighter than OR. Without parentheses, A AND B OR C reads as (A AND B) OR C, which would drag in every event where C is true regardless of type. Wrap the OR so it is one condition.

explain.meaning: Either role may hold the address. The parentheses keep both alternatives inside the event-type filter.
ip = "10.9.4.22" does the same job in one token. Both forms pass here because they return the same evidence.

hints: Either alternative may be true, so the word between them is OR, not AND.
Fill the gap with OR and keep the parentheses.

call.prompt: You drop the parentheses and the count jumps to hundreds. What happened?

options.label: Search ignored the OR and treated the three conditions as one long AND, matching far more than intended
The query became (type AND principal) OR target, so every event with that target IP, of any type, was added
The grouped field ip was triggered by the repeated address and matched both roles at once across every event type

call.why: Operator precedence silently changed the question. The results looked plausible, which is the dangerous part.

missions.clue: Twenty-one connections. Nineteen are the evening's ordinary browsing and mail. Two are the 18:52 and 18:53 connections to 203.0.113.44 that followed the phishing link. Hal's machine is a victim's machine, not the attacker's.
missions.caveat: principal.ip and target.ip are repeated fields in real UDM. This trainer models one value each; the docs cover how repeated values and negation interact.

missions.title: The one big upload
missions.beat: Beacons are small. Theft is not. Find any connection tonight that sent more than ten megabytes out. Bytes are plain numbers; compare them like numbers.
missions.question: Where did the large outbound transfer go?

concept.title: sent_bytes is from the principal's point of view
concept.text: network.sent_bytes counts what the principal transmitted to the target. A workstation that sends 48 MB to an outside address in one connection has uploaded something. Received bytes would mean a download. Read the direction before you say which.

hints: A numeric comparison: the sent-bytes field greater than ten million, written as a bare number.
network.sent_bytes > 10000000 with the connection event type.

answer.prompt: What is the target.ip of the large transfer?

call.prompt: One connection: 48,230,112 bytes sent from AUTOMATION-01 to the attacker address at 02:10, five minutes after donors_export.zip was written. What can you state, and what remains inference?

options.label: State: the donor list was stolen at 02:10. The size, the timing and the file name together prove what the stream contained
State: nothing, since the connection was encrypted and the bytes cannot be read back from the log or the sensor
State: a 48 MB upload to the attacker address followed the zip. Inference: the zip's contents were the payload

call.why: You can prove the size, the direction, the destination and the timing. Proving what was inside the stream needs the file itself or the attacker's server, neither of which you have.

missions.clue: One connection over ten megabytes all night: 48 MB from the playout PC to 203.0.113.44 at 02:10:33. The pirate segment at 03:10 read donor names on air. The donor list left the building an hour before that. The broadcast was the announcement, not the theft.
missions.caveat: Byte counts depend on the sensor. Flow logs, proxies and EDR disagree by headers and retransmits. Treat a size as approximate and the direction as reliable.
